A lanyard is a strap or cord that you wear around your neck (or sometimes your wrist) to hold or carry a small object. Think of it as a wearable holder — it keeps something important close to your body and easy to reach, without you having to put it in a pocket or bag.

A lanyard is typically a flat, ribbon-like strip (or sometimes a round cord) about 45–60 cm long (roughly the distance from your shoulder to your waist), forming a loop that sits comfortably around your neck. At the bottom of this loop, there is usually a small metal or plastic clip or hook — this is where the object gets attached.

The strap itself is most commonly made from nylon, polyester, or cotton. It can be a plain single colour, or it can have text, logos, and patterns printed on it.

The whole point of a lanyard is to keep something dangling at chest level, visible and accessible. The most common things attached to a lanyard are:

  • ID cards or access badges — so employees, students, or event attendees can display their identity at all times
  • Keys — so you don't lose them
  • USB drives — small and easy to misplace otherwise
  • Whistles — very common for sports coaches, referees, and lifeguards
  • Small tools or devices — like a small torch or a camera
Where You'll See Lanyards in Real Life

The most familiar place is at offices and workplaces, where employees hang their ID badge from a lanyard so it's always visible. Security staff can simply glance at your chest to verify who you are.

At conferences, exhibitions, and events, every participant typically receives a lanyard with a name tag or entry pass attached — it's one of the first things handed to you at the registration desk.

At schools and universities, students often carry their ID cards on lanyards. In some institutions, wearing your ID on a lanyard is mandatory.

Sports environments are full of lanyards too — a referee's whistle almost always hangs from one.
An Important Feature: The Safety Breakaway

Many modern lanyards have a small breakaway clasp — a section near the back of the neck that snaps apart easily if the lanyard gets caught on something or is pulled sharply. This is a safety feature to prevent choking or injury. Once it snaps open, you can simply press the two pieces back together and it's re-connected. If you look closely at lanyards worn by hospital staff or factory workers, you'll almost always find this feature.

A common variation is the retractable lanyard, where the cord connecting the clip to the strap is coiled inside a small plastic housing. You can pull the card out to swipe it through a card reader, and the cord automatically retracts and pulls the card back when you let go. Office workers who need to tap their badge against a door scanner multiple times a day use these constantly.

While "lanyard" almost always brings to mind a neck strap, the word also covers straps worn around the wrist. A small loop of cord attached to a camera, a TV remote, a gaming controller, or a key — designed so the object doesn't fall and get damaged if you lose your grip — is also correctly called a lanyard. You'll see this wrist-loop version on most Nintendo controllers, ski poles, and professional cameras.
How It's Different from Similar Things

• A necklace is jewellery; a lanyard is a practical, functional tool.
  • A keychain attaches to a belt loop or sits in your pocket; a lanyard goes around the neck or wrist and keeps the object at chest level or in your hand.
  • A badge holder is just the clear plastic sleeve that holds the card; the lanyard is the strap that the badge holder clips onto.
A lanyard is a strap or cord worn around the neck or wrist, fitted with a clip at one end, used to hold and display objects like ID cards, keys, or whistles so they are always accessible and visible.
